raw.assessment: The incumbent works better with stable assignments: those files had seven-minute median handling, below target. Overall accuracy was 80%, below 95%, and median handling was 17 minutes. Changes and renames characterize all eight affected exports but do not establish causation. The isolation finding has a concrete limit: the split-course center was excluded. Fast execution does not explain replacement delays or their contribution to handling time.

openings.claim: Current instructor assignments may select incorrect courses for historical weeks; renames may instead make present courses appear absent during comparison.
openings.delta: Distinguish missing course identities from mismatched names before choosing historical selection rules or clearer identification.
openings.prediction: Week-effective membership would restore genuinely missing identities; reconciling names would resolve apparent omissions without changing membership. Persistent disagreement after both would weaken this account.
openings.probe: Compare staging exports with specified weekly rosters for fabricated unchanged, reassigned, renamed, and split courses. Have coordinators identify discrepancies using their schedule practices. Keep records private, retain the CSV schema, and check tenant separation and concurrent attendance entry. Bound diagnosis and any selected fix to six engineer-days and existing hosting.
assumptions: Historical data and reliable expected rosters may be unavailable; production repair depends on feasibility.

openings.claim: Is excess handling concentrated in checking course identity, spreadsheet import, or requesting and following up on replacements?
openings.delta: Separate active work from elapsed replacement waiting to locate the useful intervention.
openings.prediction: Checking-dominated time favors identification work; import-dominated time favors import guidance; follow-up-dominated time favors replacement access. Long passive waits alone would not predict reduced handling minutes from faster delivery.
openings.probe: Use six coordinators' two short sessions to time private fabricated stable and changed-course CSV workflows, counterbalancing order. Record checking, correction, download, import, and replacement-request actions separately; distinguish job runtime from delivery delay using logs. Include this within the same six-day budget without interrupting attendance entry.
assumptions: Fabricated sessions approximate routine actions; validate improvements against the next 40 exports and all three success measures.

raw.assessment: Assignment changes and renames cluster among affected exports, but their causal role and the sources of handling time remain unmeasured. One artifact-centered hypothesis merits a bounded probe; feasibility depends on existing course identifiers and historical information.

openings.claim: Move course-set checking into a private, center-and-week manifest keyed by stable course identifiers. Treat assignment changes, renames, and splits as signals that mark only the affected manifest entries for review. The export reads the reviewed manifest, applies center authorization independently, and emits the existing CSV schema.
openings.delta: Parent mechanisms are an explicit expected-set artifact and event-driven invalidation. Their interaction converts disruptive edits into targeted review information instead of silent membership drift. A speculative capability would reconstruct the intended weekly course set automatically; it requires dated identity/assignment history, split lineage, and an authoritative definition of intent. The presently testable fragment is a coordinator-reviewed manifest plus detection of changed entries, without automatic intent reconstruction.
openings.prediction: If identity or assignment drift drives the observed omissions, manifest-based exports will retain intended courses after assignment changes and renames while reducing repeated full-list checks. If most time instead lies in importing, handling time may remain above 12 minutes.
openings.probe: Use fabricated staging cases for unchanged courses, assignment changes, renames, splits, and foreign-center identifiers. Counterbalance current and manifest workflows across the six coordinators’ two sessions; measure checking, correction, download, and import time separately and compare intended versus exported course IDs. Exercise attendance entry during generation and verify documented CSV import. Count manifest maintenance time. Before deployment, establish a six-engineer-day implementation estimate and unchanged hosting cost; then evaluate the stipulated next-40-export targets.
assumptions: Stable identifiers and a bounded way to record weekly intent exist or fit the six-day limit.
All participant processing stays within the existing private service and authorized workspaces; manifest approval never grants center access.
Generation can use an existing nonblocking read mechanism with a stated cutoff.
Missing edit signals, stale intent, or ambiguous split lineage defeat automatic checking and require explicit coordinator resolution; current assignments alone cannot reconstruct history.

critiques.assumption: A reviewed expected roster and change signals together identify every entry needing reconsideration.
critiques.limitation: The supported limitation is missing evidence of intent coverage: D1-O6 gives heterogeneous schedule sources, and their completeness and update timing are explicitly unmeasured. Z1's specified staging rosters supply that missing ground truth; A1's targeted invalidation could miss a timetable-only change or an already-wrong baseline. Those failure scenarios are conjectural, not observed.
critiques.opening: Test whether coordinators can establish weekly intent cheaply before investing in automatic historical reconstruction.
critiques.comparison: An expected-set artifact preserves an approved baseline but can preserve mistakes. Event-driven invalidation highlights captured changes but cannot detect missing intent. Their interaction enables targeted reapproval only when baseline and event coverage are adequate. Its failure boundary is stale or ambiguous intent outside captured events, particularly splits. Z1 diagnoses export disagreement only relative to its supplied roster; it does not establish that roster's authority.
critiques.probe: Proposed only: include a fabricated late timetable-only change and ambiguous split alongside captured edits; inspect whether either workflow silently accepts an incorrect set. No world test has been performed.

openings.claim: A smallest assessable capability is a private weekly intent record showing confirmed and unresolved course identities, source, and confirmation time; uncertainty triggers explicit coordinator resolution rather than inferred membership.
openings.delta: Add intent-establishment cost and uncaptured changes to A1's manifest trial. Automatic reconstruction remains dependent on dated history, split lineage, and an authoritative intent rule, none established here.
openings.prediction: If uncertainty is sparse and cheaply resolved, selective confirmation may reduce total handling; widespread ambiguity may erase savings despite correct exports.
openings.probe: Proposed: counterbalance current and intent-record workflows in the six coordinators' two fabricated staging sessions. Count confirmation, maintenance, correction, and import time; score intended versus exported IDs and foreign-center rows. Preserve documented CSV import and concurrent attendance entry. Budget the entire first change within six engineer-days and existing hosting. Any later field evaluation must reach median handling <=12 minutes, >=38/40 intended course sets, and zero foreign-center records.
openings.fit: preserves outcome and constraints; implementation feasibility remains unverified
assumptions: Intent can be resolved by an authorized coordinator.
Stable identity mapping fits the budget; otherwise this remains a manual staging probe.
All participant processing remains inside the private service and authorized workspaces.
